How does radiation melt things? I watched a Vice documentary on Chernobyl and there was an area that would literally melt your shoes if you walked on it for too long.

Great question!

Nuclear Radiation has many components that can ionize atoms ranging from the release of Alpha Particles to the release of high energy neutrons. Neutrons, the most damaging aspect of nuclear radiation, require a lot of energy to be knocked out of a nucleus and thus, we rarely see such damaging radiation outside of reactors or locations of reactor meltdowns. In the case of Chernobyl, there are undoubtedly areas still with large amounts of highly unstable heavy atoms like Uranium. When these nuclei decay spontaneously, the neutrons that fly off collide and damage almost everything in their path. When they collide, the energy they carried is converted into heat. When this happens in your shoes, your shoes will start to melt...eventually.

Dang, so it literally creates heat. Is the heat that is converted from the nuclei's energy measured in Fahrenheit/Celsius? I would assume that the temperature can get really hot. I've read that parts of the Chernobyl Power Plant were literally a sludge of melted down, irradiated metal/concrete.

Heat is the energy itself as it moves from a higher temp to a low temp. So heat itself is not measured in F or C. But yes, the temperature change is still measured the same. The heat we see here is due to the change in internal energy caused by the radiation.
